cases.case_name: Shepherd v. Clemens
cases.holding: Reversing the Family Court, the Delaware Supreme Court held that a termination petition requires proof of an enumerated statutory ground before the court may reach best interests, and that clear and convincing evidence established abandonment by the biological father and that termination served the child's best interest.
cases.quote: This Court has consistently held that the best interest element of the statute can be considered only after there has been a finding of an enumerated statutory basis for termination.

relevance.OUT-02: States Delaware's sequencing rule for termination: the best-interest inquiry is legally unavailable until an enumerated ground under 13 Del. C. section 1103(a) is found.

cases.case_name: Powell v. Department of Services for Children, Youth & Their Families
cases.holding: Affirming termination, the Court held that both steps of Delaware's two-step termination analysis must be proved by clear and convincing evidence, and that the Family Court may consider the record of earlier dependency proceedings provided it reconsiders that evidence under the higher standard.
cases.quote: Both steps must be established by clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.DEC-05: Fixes the evidentiary standard the agency must ultimately satisfy once a dependency petition is filed and the case proceeds toward termination.
relevance.ACT-02: Holds that a parent's failure to achieve case-plan goals such as housing and employment does not by itself show that DFS failed to make reasonable efforts.
relevance.ACT-03: Confirms that dependency findings made by a preponderance when the child entered foster care may be carried forward only if reweighed under the clear and convincing standard.
relevance.OUT-02: The controlling Delaware statement that both the statutory ground and the best-interests determination require clear and convincing evidence.

cases.case_name: Division of Family Services v. Harrison
cases.holding: The Court affirmed an award of guardianship to foster parents, holding that foster parents have standing to petition for guardianship of a child placed with them and that DFS, not the foster parents, bore the burden of proving the child was no longer dependent before reunification could proceed.
cases.quote: We hold that foster parents have standing to petition for guardianship of foster children under their care.

relevance.INP-04: Shows the Family Court, not the agency, controls whether a child's dependency status continues once a petition is before it.
relevance.INP-11: Illustrates that Delaware's Family Court exercises its dependency jurisdiction under 10 Del. C. section 901(8) irrespective of the agency's own placement plan.
relevance.ACT-03: Establishes that a child's foster placement can be defended in court by the foster parents themselves when the agency moves to reunify.
relevance.ACT-04: Supports a caregiver's independent standing to seek permanency for a child already in their care.
relevance.DEC-05: Allocates the burden of proof to DFS to show a child is no longer dependent when it seeks to end court involvement.
relevance.OUT-03: The leading Delaware authority recognizing foster-parent standing to obtain guardianship as a permanency outcome.
relevance.OUT-04: Demonstrates that continued court-supervised care may be ordered where the agency cannot prove the child's dependency has ended.
relevance.OUT-05: Dismissal or closure cannot rest on the agency's say-so; DFS must carry the burden that dependency has ended.
relevance.FAIL-01: A reviewing court will not disturb Family Court findings that are the product of an orderly and logical deductive process, which frames when agency decisions are overturned.

cases.case_name: Wilson v. Division of Family Services
cases.holding: The Court affirmed terminations entered on the father's written consent, holding that a consent is valid if made knowingly, voluntarily and intelligently and that due process does not require the Family Court to repeat a verbal colloquy where a properly executed written consent was signed with counsel.
cases.quote: Therefore, a consent to the termination of parental rights must be made knowingly, voluntarily and intelligently.

relevance.OUT-02: Governs consent terminations in Delaware and defines the validity test a parent must meet to later attack a consent.

cases.case_name: Stewart v. Department of Services for Children, Youth, & Their Families
cases.holding: Affirming termination and the denial of two relatives' guardianship petitions, the Court held that a guardianship petitioner must show by a preponderance both that the child is dependent or neglected and that guardianship is in the child's best interests, and that DFS made appropriate reunification services available to a mother with mental disabilities.
cases.quote: To grant a guardianship petition, two factors must be shown by the preponderance of the evidence

relevance.INP-05: Addresses what happens when relatives come forward asking to take responsibility for a child already in agency custody.
relevance.DEC-06: Shows the court testing whether services offered short of removal were adequate to the parent's actual needs.
relevance.ACT-01: Measures the adequacy of voluntary and agency-arranged services against the parent's documented limitations.
relevance.ACT-02: Holds that the reunification services DFS offers must be appropriate to the parent's condition, here a cognitive disability.
relevance.ACT-03: Frames the comparison between continued foster placement and a relative's guardianship petition.
relevance.ACT-04: States the two-element preponderance test a relative must satisfy to obtain guardianship over the agency's objection.
relevance.OUT-01: Defines when reunification services have been adequately made available so that reunification can be ruled out.
relevance.OUT-03: The controlling Delaware statement of the guardianship standard and its burden of proof.
relevance.OUT-04: Relevant where continued agency custody rather than relative guardianship determines a youth's path to permanency.
relevance.FAIL-05: Addresses a disability-based claim that the agency's case plan failed to accommodate the parent.

cases.case_name: Clark v. Division of Family Services
cases.holding: The Court affirmed termination, holding that the mother's conviction of a felony-level offense against a child under 13 Del. C. section 1103(a)(4) independently satisfied the statutory-ground step of the required two-step analysis, so the failure-to-plan ground need not be reached.
cases.quote: Before terminating a parent's rights in a child, the Family Court must engage in a two-step analysis.

relevance.ACT-02: Shows the point at which a felony conviction against a child and incarceration can end the agency's reunification-service obligation.
relevance.ACT-04: Decided alongside relatives' competing guardianship petitions, illustrating how kinship options are weighed against termination.

cases.case_name: Stearns v. Division of Family Services
cases.holding: The Court affirmed, holding that a parent who presents evidence after her Family Court Civil Rule 41(b) motion to dismiss is denied waives the right to contest that denial on appeal, and that the trial judge adequately addressed the best-interest factors.
cases.quote: By presenting evidence to support her defense after the Family Court judge denied her Motion to Dismiss, Stearns waived her right to contest the dismissal.

relevance.DEC-05: Defines the mid-trial test of whether the agency's petition evidence suffices, and how that challenge is preserved.
relevance.OUT-05: The Delaware rule on moving to dismiss an agency petition for insufficient evidence and the waiver trap that follows.
relevance.FAIL-01: Explains why many agency-decision challenges fail on appeal for want of preservation rather than on the merits.

cases.case_name: Hunt v. Division of Family Services
cases.holding: On expedited interlocutory appeal the Court affirmed, holding that the Family Court's statutory authority to consent to medical care for a child in DFS custody carries with it the authority to de-escalate treatment and withdraw life support, and that both parents received procedural due process.
cases.quote: Accordingly, we hold that the Family Court's authority to de-escalate medical treatment and to withdraw life support is a logical corollary to its statutory authority to consent to medical care.

relevance.INP-07: Arises from a hospital's identification of non-accidental trauma and defines the court's role once medical findings enter the dependency case.
relevance.ACT-06: The controlling Delaware authority on who may authorize or withdraw emergency medical intervention for a child in agency custody.
relevance.OUT-06: Sets the procedure and due-process protections applicable when a case reaches catastrophic injury and end-of-life decisions.
relevance.PMC-04: A case of catastrophic non-accidental injury under court supervision, the fact pattern fatality review is meant to capture.

cases.case_name: Short v. Department of Services for Children, Youth & Their Families
cases.holding: The Court affirmed termination of the father's rights, holding that the Family Court properly found an enumerated statutory ground under 13 Del. C. section 1103(a) before weighing the section 722 best-interest factors.
cases.quote: First, the Family Court must find that one of the grounds for termination enumerated in title 13, section 1103(a) has been established.

relevance.OUT-02: Restates the required first step of Delaware's termination analysis and the statute that supplies the grounds.

cases.case_name: Sampson v. Division of Family Services
cases.holding: The Court affirmed termination, holding that 13 Del. C. section 1103(a)(6), which permits termination where the parent's rights over a sibling were involuntarily terminated in a prior proceeding, affords sufficient due process because each statutory element must still be proved by clear and convincing evidence and the parent is represented and heard.
cases.quote: We conclude that Section 1103(a)(6) affords sufficient due process.

relevance.DEC-03: Upholds the use of a prior adverse agency-driven finding as a statutory predicate, while requiring that each element be proved anew by clear and convincing evidence.

cases.case_name: Waters v. Division of Family Services
cases.holding: The Court reversed the termination of the father's parental rights, holding that the State denied him procedural due process by terminating without first providing any meaningful case plan or attempting feasible reunification, and that the abandonment finding was not supported by clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: Ashley was entitled to a timely permanency decision, but in these circumstances that entitlement could not trump her father's due process right to a reasonable opportunity for reunification.

relevance.INP-05: Applies where a parent seeks involvement and services but the agency never opens a plan for him.
relevance.DEC-06: Shows that skipping the service-and-plan stage altogether is a due-process defect, not merely a programmatic choice.
relevance.ACT-01: Establishes that the offer of a workable plan and services is constitutionally significant, not optional.
relevance.ACT-02: The leading Delaware holding that DFS must provide a meaningful case plan and feasible reunification services before seeking termination.
relevance.OUT-01: Holds that a parent must be given a reasonable opportunity for reunification before that outcome is foreclosed.
relevance.FAIL-01: A direct example of the Delaware Supreme Court reversing an agency-driven termination for procedural due-process failure.

cases.case_name: Division of Family Services v. James
cases.holding: The Family Court denied the Division's motion to be relieved of offering reunification services to a mother whose rights to a sibling had been involuntarily terminated, holding that the decision whether reasonable efforts are required rests with the court rather than the agency, and ordering reunification to remain the permanency goal.
cases.quote: In either case, judicial authority to keep secure a child's best interest throughout a case can never be interrupted or, even for a brief point in time, delegated elsewhere.

relevance.INP-04: Confirms that once a dependency case is opened the court, not the Division, directs what the agency must do next.
relevance.INP-05: Applies where a parent is actively working a plan and the agency nevertheless seeks to stop services.
relevance.INP-10: Shows that escalation of the agency's internal committee recommendation does not bind the court.
relevance.INP-12: Sets out the preliminary protective hearing framework, including the ten-day timeline and probable-cause standard governing continued emergency custody.
relevance.DEC-04: Explains the probable-cause review that must follow an ex parte emergency custody order under Family Court Civil Rule 212(a).
relevance.DEC-05: Describes the adjudicatory sequence after a petition is filed and the preponderance standard for a dependency finding.
relevance.DEC-06: Demonstrates the court preserving a service-based, non-termination track over the agency's objection.
relevance.ACT-01: Ordered the Division to continue offering the services in the tendered case plan while its motion was pending.
relevance.ACT-02: The key Delaware trial-court holding that only the court may excuse DFS from making reasonable efforts.
relevance.ACT-05: Illustrates the court's continuing authority to shape protective conditions rather than delegating them to the agency.
relevance.OUT-01: Reinstated reunification as the permanency goal where the mother demonstrated substantial change.
relevance.OUT-05: Shows the court refusing to let an agency motion foreclose a case outcome the record did not support.
relevance.FAIL-01: A direct example of a court rejecting an agency's no-reasonable-efforts determination.
relevance.PMC-01: Bears on the reasonable-efforts judicial determinations that drive Title IV-E and CFSR compliance.
relevance.PMC-03: Shows agency internal committees operating without documented policy criteria, precisely the practice citizen review panels are meant to examine.

cases.case_name: Department of Services for Children, Youth, & Their Families v. Garcias
cases.holding: The Family Court terminated both parents' rights, holding that DFS proved by clear and convincing evidence the mother's failure to plan, the father's abandonment, and that the Division had made reasonable efforts to reunify the family.
cases.quote: Given the importance of the rights at stake and the permanent nature of this proceeding, DFS must prove these elements by clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.ACT-02: States that where the ground is failure to plan the court must review whether DFS developed a meaningful case plan and made reasonable efforts.
relevance.OUT-01: Sets out the reasonable-efforts finding that must precede a conclusion that reunification is no longer viable.
relevance.FAIL-03: Shows the judicial reasonable-efforts determination on which Title IV-E federal reimbursement depends.
relevance.PMC-01: A worked example of the reasonable-efforts and permanency findings CFSR reviews measure.

cases.case_name: Division of Family Services v. Redman
cases.holding: The Family Court granted the Division's motion to quash a parent's Rule 45 subpoena duces tecum for the Division's case file, holding that a trial subpoena is not the proper vehicle and that access must instead proceed through an expedited discovery request consistent with the Division's federal and state confidentiality obligations.
cases.quote: For the reasons that will follow, the Court is granting the Division's Motion to Quash the subpoena which was issued pursuant to Family Court Civil Rule 45.

relevance.INP-09: Defines the confidentiality constraints that limit outside inspection of DFS case records.
relevance.FAIL-06: The Delaware authority on when the Division may and may not withhold its records, and the procedure a party must use to compel them.
relevance.PMC-02: Sets the confidentiality boundary any auditor or reviewer of DFS files must work within.
relevance.PMC-05: Establishes that DFS records are confidential by federal and state law, so transparency must be pursued through the procedures the court identifies.
relevance.PMC-06: Shows the court balancing confidentiality against the permanency and reunification interests that argue for disclosure.

cases.case_name: Division of Family Services v. A.B.
cases.holding: The Family Court held a substance-abuse treatment provider in civil contempt and fined it for failing to produce a mother's records in response to the court's good-cause disclosure order and subpoena duces tecum, notwithstanding the federal confidentiality rules governing such records.
cases.quote: Furthermore, in a civil contempt proceeding, it is not a defense that the party in contempt did not have subjective intent to violate the Court's Order.

relevance.INP-07: Governs how a treatment provider's records reach a dependency case and the releases and good-cause orders required.
relevance.ACT-06: Defines the disclosure mechanics when a court-ordered treatment or evaluation is part of the case plan.
relevance.FAIL-06: Shows the sanction available when an entity fails to disclose records a court has ordered produced.
relevance.PMC-05: Sets out the federal 42 U.S.C. 290dd-2 good-cause standard weighing public interest and need for disclosure against patient injury.

cases.case_name: S.L. v. A.L.
cases.holding: The Family Court dismissed a minor's emancipation petition for want of subject-matter jurisdiction, holding that the Family Court is a court of limited statutory jurisdiction and cannot entertain a proceeding for which the Delaware Code supplies no statutory basis.
cases.quote: Therefore, in order for this Court to find jurisdiction over a Petition for Emancipation, the Delaware Code must provide the Court with a statutory basis for the proceeding.

relevance.INP-04: Defines the outer limit of what a court may order the Family Court to entertain: only proceedings the Code creates.
relevance.INP-11: Confirms that Family Court jurisdiction is statutory, so any federal or tribal jurisdictional overlay must be located in an enabling provision.
relevance.OUT-03: Relevant to whether a requested permanency arrangement falls within an existing statutory cause of action.
relevance.OUT-04: The closest Delaware authority on a youth's own petition to alter custodial status as majority approaches, and the jurisdictional predicate such a petition requires.

cases.case_name: Doe 30's Mother v. Bradley
cases.holding: The Superior Court dismissed the common-law duty claims against physicians and the Medical Society, holding that Delaware's Medical Practice Act and Child Abuse Prevention Act reporting statutes do not create a new affirmative tort duty to report and cannot support negligence per se absent a pre-existing common-law duty.
cases.quote: the Court will not recognize a new affirmative common law tort duty stemming from the statutory language of the MPA or CAPA

relevance.INP-01: The central Delaware decision on what a mandatory reporter's statutory duty under 16 Del. C. section 903 does and does not create in tort.
relevance.INP-02: Confirms the reporting statute reaches any person who knows or in good faith suspects abuse, while limiting the private remedy for failing to report.
relevance.INP-06: Bears on the consequences of a suspicion never routed to the hotline: a statutory violation without a new common-law duty.
relevance.INP-07: Arises directly from physicians who suspected a colleague's abuse of child patients and did not report.
relevance.INP-08: Applies the same analysis to any professional reporter whose failure to report is alleged to have caused harm.
relevance.DEC-01: Explains why an unreported or unscreened suspicion generally yields no private tort claim in Delaware.
relevance.FAIL-04: Defines the narrow path to civil liability where a failure to report preceded continued abuse of children.

cases.case_name: Flowers, Jr. v. Office of the Governor
cases.holding: On appeal from the Chief Deputy Attorney General's FOIA determination, the Superior Court held that the burden of proof rests on the public body to give sufficient reasons for withholding records and found that the Governor's Office satisfied that burden under the legislative e-mail and privilege exemptions.
cases.quote: Regardless of who reviews the requestor's petition, the burden of proof is on the public body to demonstrate that its "reasons" for withholding records were sufficient.

relevance.INP-09: Supplies the mechanism by which oversight bodies and the public obtain agency records that can trigger scrutiny.
relevance.FAIL-06: The controlling Delaware statement that a withholding agency, not the requester, bears the burden of justifying nondisclosure.
relevance.PMC-02: Defines the state-law route to the records an audit or financial review would need.
relevance.PMC-03: Supports independent review panels' access to agency records by placing the justification burden on the agency.
relevance.PMC-05: The core Delaware FOIA authority on burden of proof, the Chief Deputy petition process, and Superior Court appeal under 29 Del. C. section 10005.
relevance.PMC-06: Establishes the legal baseline for any public-facing dashboard built on Delaware agency records.

cases.case_name: Croft v. Westmoreland County Children and Youth Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
cases.holding: The Third Circuit reversed summary judgment for the caseworker, holding that a caseworker who lacked objectively reasonable grounds to believe a child had been abused or was in imminent danger violated the family's Fourteenth Amendment liberty interest by forcing the father to leave the home under threat of removal.
cases.quote: Even considered together, minor inconsistencies which provide no affirmative evidence of sexual abuse cannot alone establish the objectively reasonable grounds necessary to remove a family member from the family unit.

relevance.INP-02: Sets the constitutional floor a third-party report must clear before the State may act coercively on it.
relevance.INP-03: Confirms that police involvement does not relieve the agency of needing objectively reasonable grounds before separating a family.
relevance.INP-06: Arose from an anonymous tip and holds that such a tip, uncorroborated, is not objectively reasonable grounds for intervention.
relevance.INP-08: Applies equally to school or professional referrals: the report must yield affirmative evidence before the family is disturbed.
relevance.INP-10: Escalation from screening to coercive intervention is judged on the information the worker actually possessed at the time.
relevance.INP-12: Protective custody or forced separation without objectively reasonable grounds violates the family's constitutional liberty interest.
relevance.DEC-01: Supports screening out where investigation produces only minor inconsistencies and no affirmative evidence of abuse.
relevance.DEC-02: Frames the investigative decision as measured objectively against what the caseworker knew when she acted.
relevance.DEC-03: A substantiation resting on inconsistencies rather than affirmative evidence cannot justify interference with parental rights.
relevance.DEC-04: The governing Third Circuit standard for the removal decision: objectively reasonable grounds of abuse or imminent danger.
relevance.ACT-05: Treats an order excluding a parent from the home as itself an interference with family integrity requiring adequate grounds.
relevance.FAIL-02: The leading Third Circuit authority that separating a family without objectively reasonable grounds is actionable under section 1983.
relevance.FAIL-05: Guards against intervention driven by suspicion rather than evidence, the mechanism by which biased referrals become removals.

cases.case_name: Miller v. City of Philadelphia
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
cases.holding: The Third Circuit affirmed judgment for the child-welfare caseworker, holding that a substantive due process claim arising from a child-welfare intervention requires executive conduct that shocks the conscience, a standard that negligence cannot meet.
cases.quote: Critically, under this standard, officials will not be held liable for actions that are merely negligent.

relevance.INP-03: Sets the fault standard for constitutional claims arising out of coordinated agency and law-enforcement intervention.
relevance.DEC-02: Establishes that an imperfect or negligent investigation is not by itself a constitutional violation.
relevance.DEC-03: Holds that an erroneous substantiation or petition, without conscience-shocking conduct, does not state a due process claim.
relevance.FAIL-02: Supplies the shocks-the-conscience fault standard that governs substantive due process removal claims in Delaware's circuit.
relevance.FAIL-04: Defines the fault threshold a family must meet when alleging that agency conduct caused a child's harm.

cases.case_name: Good v. Dauphin County Social Services For Children And Youth
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
cases.holding: The Third Circuit held that a state child-protective-services immunity statute cannot shield defendants from federal claims, and that a warrantless entry into a home and strip search of a child by a caseworker and police required either freely given consent or exigent circumstances, precluding summary judgment.
cases.quote: We conclude that: 1) Pennsylvania's Child Protective Services Law cannot immunize defendants from a suit alleging a violation of a federal law

relevance.INP-01: Holds that state reporter and investigator immunity statutes cannot bar federal constitutional claims.
relevance.INP-02: Confirms that acting on a third-party report does not by itself supply lawful authority to enter a home.
relevance.INP-03: Directly addresses a caseworker accompanied by police entering and searching without a warrant.
relevance.INP-06: Shows that a hotline report alone does not create exigency justifying warrantless entry.
relevance.INP-08: Applies to any referral-driven home visit: entry requires freely given consent or exigent circumstances.
relevance.INP-10: Marks the constitutional line an investigation crosses when it becomes a search of the home or the child's body.
relevance.INP-12: Holds that the emergency exception must rest on a genuine need to protect life or avoid serious bodily injury.
relevance.DEC-02: Defines the Fourth Amendment limits on how a child-abuse investigation may be conducted.
relevance.FAIL-02: Establishes that unlawful entry and search in a child-protective investigation are actionable in federal court despite state immunity.

cases.case_name: Mammaro v. New Jersey Division of Child Protection & Permanency
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
cases.holding: The Third Circuit reversed the denial of qualified immunity, holding that no clearly established law put caseworkers on notice that temporarily removing a child after the parent left approved housing violated substantive due process.
cases.quote: We conclude that there was no consensus of authority that temporarily removing a child after the parent takes the child from approved housing violates substantive due process.

relevance.INP-12: Shows how narrowly a court frames the right at issue when emergency custody is challenged after the fact.
relevance.DEC-04: Defines the qualified-immunity limits on damages claims arising from a temporary removal decision.
relevance.FAIL-02: The current Third Circuit statement that caseworkers are immune from removal claims absent clearly established law on the specific conduct.

cases.case_name: B.S. Ex Rel. T.S. v. Somerset County
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
cases.holding: The Third Circuit held that the county violated the mother's procedural due process rights by never affording her a prompt post-removal hearing, while affirming that the caseworker's substantive due process conduct and absolute immunity defenses were properly resolved for the defendants.
cases.quote: Speaking generally, however, it should be obvious that a hearing 40 days later is not sufficiently prompt.

relevance.INP-12: Establishes that emergency custody triggers a constitutional right to be promptly heard after the child is taken.
relevance.DEC-04: Holds that the removal decision must be followed by a prompt post-removal hearing regardless of state-law procedure.
relevance.ACT-03: Confirms that the timing of judicial review after a child enters foster care is itself a constitutional requirement.
relevance.FAIL-02: Establishes municipal section 1983 liability where no prompt post-removal hearing was ever offered.

cases.case_name: Santosky v. Kramer
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed, holding that a preponderance standard is constitutionally insufficient and that due process requires at least clear and convincing evidence before a State may terminate parental rights.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.DEC-05: Sets the federal constitutional floor that shapes the evidentiary path from dependency petition to termination.
relevance.OUT-02: The controlling federal standard of proof for termination, which Delaware's clear and convincing rule implements.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Servs. of Durham Cty.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court affirmed, holding that the Due Process Clause does not require appointed counsel in every parental termination proceeding and that the need for counsel is to be decided case by case under the Mathews factors.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.DEC-05: Frames the federal right-to-counsel floor that applies once the State files to sever the parent-child relationship.
relevance.FAIL-01: Supplies the federal baseline against which a claim of uncounselled or unfair proceedings is measured on review.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court affirmed, holding that the Due Process Clause imposes no general affirmative duty on a State to protect a child from private violence, even where the agency knew of the danger and failed to act.
cases.quote: As a general matter, then, we conclude that a State's failure to protect an individual against private violence simply does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause.

relevance.OUT-06: The controlling federal rule that agency inaction preceding a child's death or injury is generally not a constitutional violation.
relevance.FAIL-03: Confirms that federal program failures do not translate into constitutional duties enforceable by individuals.
relevance.FAIL-04: The leading federal authority a family encounters when suing over a child's death after agency knowledge of the risk.
relevance.PMC-04: Explains why fatality review, rather than constitutional litigation, is the operative accountability mechanism.

cases.case_name: Stanley v. Illinois
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed, holding that a State may not take children from an unwed father, presumed unfit by statute, without a hearing on his actual fitness as a parent.
cases.quote: Under the Due Process Clause that advantage is insufficient to justify refusing a father a hearing when the issue at stake is the dismemberment of his family.

relevance.INP-12: Establishes that administrative convenience cannot justify taking children without an individualized hearing.
relevance.DEC-04: Requires that a removal predicated on presumed unfitness be tested at a hearing on actual fitness.
relevance.ACT-05: Confirms that protective measures separating a parent from a child must rest on individualized findings.
relevance.FAIL-02: The foundational federal holding that removal without a fitness hearing violates due process.

cases.case_name: Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed, holding that ICWA section 1912(f) does not bar termination where the parent never had custody, that section 1912(d)'s active-efforts requirement applies only where termination would precipitate the breakup of an existing Indian family, and that section 1915(a)'s placement preferences do not apply when no preferred party has sought to adopt.
cases.quote: Consistent with the statutory text, we hold that §1912(d) applies only in cases where an Indian family's "breakup" would be precipitated by the termination of the parent's rights.

relevance.INP-11: The governing federal construction of ICWA's active-efforts and placement-preference provisions, which supplies the standard for Delaware because no published Delaware ICWA decision was located.

cases.case_name: In re Burns
cases.holding: The Court reversed the termination of a young mother's parental rights and returned custody of her son to her, holding that requiring an unrepresented minor to sign a voluntary placement agreement as the price of housing assistance, followed by an ex parte custody order entered without the notice the rules required, fell below minimum due process, and that the agencies' failure to provide meaningful case plans or make reasonable efforts to prevent removal and reunify the family independently vitiated the judgment.
cases.quote: DCPS must prove by clear and convincing evidence that termination of parental rights is essential to the child's welfare.

relevance.INP-05: Arises from a homeless teenage mother who went to the agency asking for help and was required to surrender custody as the condition of getting it.
relevance.ACT-01: Holds that a nominally voluntary placement agreement extracted from an unrepresented minor, as a Hobson's choice against losing her child, cannot satisfy due process.
relevance.OUT-01: Returns custody to the mother because the State never made the reasonable efforts to prevent removal and reunify that must precede foreclosing reunification.
relevance.FAIL-01: The foundational Delaware Supreme Court reversal of an agency-driven termination, resting on both due-process defects and the absence of reasonable efforts.
relevance.FAIL-03: Delaware's leading statement of what Titles IV-B and IV-E demand of the State - meaningful case plans and affirmative preventive and reunification services - as the price of federal funds.
relevance.PMC-01: Identifies the judicial reasonable-efforts determinations on which Title IV-E reimbursement and CFSR performance review both depend.

cases.case_name: In re Hanks
cases.holding: The Court affirmed the termination of a chronically mentally ill mother's parental rights, holding that the words "plan" and "adequately" in the failure-to-plan ground of 13 Del. C. section 1103(5) are not unconstitutionally vague, that the State had made repeated attempts to preserve the family before seeking termination, and that the record supported the Family Court's best-interest determination under the 13 Del. C. section 722(a) factors.
cases.quote: In addition, judicial decisions clearly indicate that termination, to be lawful, must be in the child's best interests.

relevance.OUT-02: Supplies the best-interest half of Delaware's two-step termination test, applying the 13 Del. C. section 722(a) factors that the brief's statutory-ground cases never reach.
relevance.ACT-04: Shows the agency's second case plan directed at placing the children with the mother's relatives, and what follows when that kinship option fails.
relevance.FAIL-05: The leading Delaware termination decision resting on a parent's severe chronic mental illness, the fact pattern in which disability-based objections to a case plan arise.

cases.case_name: Brown v. Division of Family Services
cases.holding: The Court reversed terminations entered against parents who never appeared, holding that state and federal due process require the Family Court, when it serves a termination petition, to include notice of the Lassiter right of an indigent parent to request counsel at State expense, and remanded for a Lassiter hearing.
cases.quote: In this case, since the parents were not advised of their right to request court-appointed counsel, we reverse the judgments of the Family Court and remand for a Lassiter hearing.

relevance.DEC-05: Delaware's own application of Lassiter: when the State files a petition to sever the parent-child relationship, the notice served with it must tell an indigent parent how and when to request appointed counsel.

cases.case_name: In re Heller
cases.holding: The Court affirmed the termination of both parents' rights, holding that the Division had no duty to attempt reunification with an incarcerated father where reunification was not feasible, that the absence of a reunification case plan for him did not preclude the Family Court's best-interest finding, and that allowing the mother to participate in the hearing by telephone did not deny her due process.
cases.quote: Before the State can intercede and deprive a parent of this fundamental liberty interest, it must afford the parent with the requisite due process protection.

relevance.ACT-02: Marks the outer limit of the reasonable-efforts duty: no reunification case plan is required where the Division reasonably determines reunification is not feasible.
relevance.ACT-03: Upholds the Division's decision to keep two siblings together in the same placement as controlling over a parent's competing claim to his child.
relevance.OUT-01: Defines when a Delaware court may find reunification properly ruled out even though no formal reunification plan was ever written.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of Kelly Stevens
cases.holding: Sitting en banc, the Court affirmed the Family Court's legal test - an enumerated statutory ground must be proved by clear and convincing evidence before best interests may be weighed, so the child's best interest cannot itself supply a ground for termination - but remanded because the record was incomplete on the biological father's good-faith efforts to establish contact and on any settled purpose to abandon.
cases.quote: In Delaware, the statutory standard is two-fold: proof of an enumerated statutory ground and a determination that severing the parental tie would be in the best interest of the child.

relevance.DEC-03: Holds that an adverse finding severing a parent's rights must rest on a statutory ground proved by clear and convincing evidence, not on a comparative judgment about which home would serve the child better.
relevance.OUT-05: The Delaware Supreme Court authority for refusing a termination petition where the statutory ground is not established, whatever the child's best interests might otherwise suggest.

cases.case_name: Nicini v. Morra
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
cases.holding: Sitting en banc, the Third Circuit held that when the State places a child in state-regulated foster care it enters a special relationship with that child carrying affirmative constitutional duties enforceable under section 1983, but affirmed judgment for the caseworker because his investigation of the placement amounted at most to negligence and did not satisfy the deliberate indifference standard.
cases.quote: when the state places a child in state-regulated foster care, the state has entered into a special relationship with that child which imposes upon it certain affirmative duties

relevance.ACT-03: The controlling circuit rule that once the State places a child in foster care it owes that child affirmative constitutional duties of care and protection.
relevance.OUT-06: Supplies the special-relationship exception to DeShaney that governs when a child is seriously harmed or killed while already in state care.
relevance.FAIL-04: Sets the deliberate-indifference fault standard a family must meet to hold a caseworker liable for harm suffered by a child in agency custody.
relevance.PMC-04: Defines the constitutional duty whose breach a fatality or serious-injury review of a child in care is actually measuring.

cases.case_name: Ernst v. Child and Youth Services of Chester County
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
cases.holding: Affirming judgment for the agency defendants on the alternative ground of immunity and reversing the judgment entered against the agency's attorney, the Third Circuit held as a matter of first impression that child-welfare workers and counsel representing child-welfare agencies are absolutely immune from section 1983 damages for actions taken in preparing for, initiating and prosecuting dependency proceedings, including formulating and presenting recommendations to the court.
cases.quote: we hold that the CYS defendants are entitled to absolute immunity for their actions on behalf of the state in preparing for, initiating, and prosecuting dependency proceedings

relevance.DEC-02: Draws the line between investigative conduct, which carries only qualified immunity, and quasi-prosecutorial case-building, which is absolutely immune from damages.
relevance.DEC-03: Holds that the caseworker's gathering and evaluation of the information underlying a dependency recommendation cannot be challenged in damages at all, however wrong the finding turns out to be.
relevance.FAIL-04: Identifies the barrier a Delaware family actually faces when suing over agency conduct that produced a petition: absolute immunity, not merely the qualified immunity the brief's other cases discuss.

cases.case_name: Mulholland v. Government County of Berks
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
cases.holding: Affirming judgment for the county, the Third Circuit held that the statutory notice, amendment and expungement procedure available to a person listed as an indicated perpetrator on the state child-abuse registry satisfies procedural due process, so the county agency's policy of not forwarding later exculpatory information to the registry was not unconstitutional, and a single caseworker's lapse could not establish municipal liability.
cases.quote: the process provided by the CPSL allows a subject of a report of child abuse the opportunity to air new information at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner

relevance.DEC-02: Holds that an allegedly desultory abuse investigation supports no municipal claim absent an agency policy or custom of conducting inadequate investigations.
relevance.DEC-03: The circuit's child-abuse-registry authority: what process is due a person recorded as an indicated perpetrator, and what the investigating agency need not do once the report is filed.

cases.case_name: Suter v. Artist M.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Reversing the Seventh Circuit, the Supreme Court held that the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's requirement that a State make reasonable efforts to prevent removal and to reunify families imposes only a generalized duty, enforceable by the Secretary through the plan-approval process, and confers no privately enforceable right under section 1983 and no implied cause of action.
cases.quote: We conclude that 42 U. S. C. § 671 (a)(15) neither confers an enforceable private right on its beneficiaries nor creates an implied cause of action on their behalf.

relevance.FAIL-03: The controlling federal rule that a State's failure to meet Title IV-E plan requirements is corrected through the Secretary's funding oversight rather than by private litigation.
relevance.OUT-04: Explains why a youth seeking continued or extended federally funded foster-care and transition services has no private federal cause of action to compel them.
relevance.PMC-01: Confirms that federal monitoring of the state plan, the mechanism CFSR implements, is what Congress provided in place of a private enforcement right.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Reversing the Mississippi Supreme Court, the Court held that "domicile" in ICWA is a uniform federal standard rather than a matter of state law, that twins born off-reservation to reservation-domiciled parents were domiciled on the reservation, and that the tribal court therefore had exclusive jurisdiction under 25 U.S.C. section 1911(a), so the state adoption decree had to be vacated.
cases.quote: Tribal jurisdiction under § 1911(a) was not meant to be defeated by the actions of individual members of the tribe

relevance.INP-11: The controlling federal decision on when ICWA strips a state court of jurisdiction altogether in favor of the tribal court, which Delaware courts must apply because Delaware has produced no ICWA case law of its own.

notes: Court structure: Delaware has NO intermediate appellate court. The tiers used here are (1) Supreme Court of Delaware (court_id del) - binding; (2) Superior Court of Delaware (delsuperct) and Family Court of Delaware (delfamct) - trial courts of record whose published opinions are persuasive, not binding; (3) U.S. Supreme Court for federal constitutional standards; (4) U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit (ca3), Delaware's circuit, for section 1983 removal/search claims.

Practice warning for families: Doe 30's Mother v. Bradley holds that Delaware's mandatory reporting statutes (16 Del. C. section 903, which makes EVERY person a reporter, and 24 Del. C. section 1731A) create NO new common-law tort duty and NO negligence per se claim. Smith v. Bunkley holds that sovereign immunity bars state-law claims against the State, DSCYF and DFS, and that CAPTA creates no private right of action. Together these close most state-court damages routes in Delaware; the surviving avenues are federal - section 1983 under the Third Circuit standards (Croft, Good, Miller, Mammaro, B.S. v. Somerset) and the Rehabilitation Act/ADA.

Practice note on removal timing: B.S. ex rel. T.S. v. Somerset County establishes a federal constitutional right to a PROMPT post-removal hearing independent of state law. Delaware's own rule (Fam. Ct. Civ. R. 212(a), quoted in DFS v. James) requires a preliminary protective hearing within 10 days of an ex parte custody order, at a probable-cause standard that may rest on hearsay; the adjudicatory hearing follows within 30 days at a preponderance standard (Fam. Ct. Civ. R. 213). Delaware's timeline therefore comfortably satisfies B.S.; the litigable question is compliance, not the rule.

Reasonable efforts: DFS v. James (Del. Fam. Ct. 2009) is the most useful Delaware authority for families - it holds that the Family Court, not the Division, decides whether reunification services may be withheld, and it rejected a Permanency Planning Committee recommendation that rested on risk factors the witness could not locate in any written policy. Waters v. DFS (Del. 2006) is its Supreme Court counterpart, reversing a termination entered without any case plan or reunification attempt.
